description: Introductory recursion in Python, as taught in a first-year programming course.

concepts.name: Recursive decomposition
concepts.description: Expressing a problem in terms of one or more smaller instances of the same problem, and trusting that the smaller instances are solved correctly.

misconceptions.description: Believes you must mentally trace every recursive call to trust the result, rather than assuming the recursive call is correct for the smaller input (the 'recursive leap of faith').
symptoms: Explanation walks through every call level instead of stating what one call does
Adds special cases for inputs of size 2 or 3 because they 'could not trace' larger ones

misconceptions.description: Splits the input into pieces that are not the same kind of problem, so the recursive call cannot actually solve them.
symptoms: Recursive call receives an element (e.g. an int) where the function expects a list
Recursive call's argument has a different type or meaning from the original parameter

concepts.name: Base case
concepts.description: A condition under which the function returns a result directly, without making a recursive call. Every recursion needs at least one reachable base case.

misconceptions.description: Omits the base case, believing the recursion will stop on its own.
symptoms: No branch returns without calling the function again
RecursionError on every input

misconceptions.description: Has a base case that returns the wrong value, often confusing the identity for the operation (e.g. returns 1 for an empty sum, or None).
symptoms: Empty input returns 1, None or the input itself instead of 0
Every result is off by a constant amount

misconceptions.description: Handles only one kind of terminating input and misses others (e.g. handles an empty list but not a non-list element).
symptoms: Works on flat or simple inputs but crashes on edge cases such as empty sublists
TypeError when the function is called on an int

concepts.name: Recursive case
concepts.description: The branch that solves the problem by calling the function on smaller input(s) and combining the results.

misconceptions.description: Makes the recursive call but does not combine its result with the current step's work.
symptoms: Returns only the recursive call's result, dropping the current element
Returns only the current element, ignoring the recursive call's result

misconceptions.description: Calls the function on the same input rather than on part of it.
symptoms: Recursive call passes the original parameter unchanged
RecursionError even though a base case exists

concepts.name: Progress towards the base case
concepts.description: Each recursive call must move the input measurably closer to a base case so the recursion is guaranteed to terminate.

misconceptions.description: Changes the input in a way that does not approach the base case (e.g. slices from the wrong end or changes an unrelated variable).
symptoms: Slice such as lst[0:] or lst[:len(lst)] that keeps the same length
Timeout or RecursionError on inputs longer than one element

misconceptions.description: Has a base case and makes progress, but the progress can skip over the base case condition.
symptoms: Base case checks len(lst) == 1 but the input can become empty
Terminates for some input sizes but not others

concepts.name: The call stack
concepts.description: Each call gets its own frame with its own local variables; frames are pushed on call and popped on return, and deep recursion can exhaust the stack.

misconceptions.description: Believes local variables are shared between recursive calls, so updating a local in a deeper call changes it in the caller.
symptoms: Accumulates into a local variable in the callee and expects the caller to see it
Explanation says 'total keeps adding up across calls' without passing or returning it

misconceptions.description: Relies on a global or default-mutable accumulator to carry state between calls, often because frames are not understood.
symptoms: global total or a def f(lst, acc=[]) default argument
Correct on the first call but wrong on repeated calls in the same process

misconceptions.description: Does not realise that each call uses stack space, so very deep recursion fails with RecursionError.
symptoms: Explanation claims recursion depth is unlimited
Surprise at RecursionError on deeply nested input despite correct logic

concepts.name: Return value propagation
concepts.description: A value returned by a deeper call goes back only to its direct caller, which must use it and return its own result in turn.

misconceptions.description: Calls the function recursively but forgets to return (or use) the result, so None comes back.
symptoms: Line like sum_nested(rest) with no return or assignment
Function returns None for non-trivial inputs, or TypeError adding int and NoneType

misconceptions.description: Believes a return in the base case sends its value straight back to the original caller, skipping intermediate frames.
symptoms: Explanation says the base case 'returns the answer to the user'
Intermediate calls do not return anything after the recursive call

misconceptions.description: Prints the result instead of returning it, treating output as the function's value.
symptoms: print(...) in the base or recursive case with no return
Correct numbers appear in stdout but tests see None

concepts.name: Recursion vs iteration
concepts.description: Knowing when a problem's structure suits recursion (e.g. nested data) or a loop, and how the two can be combined correctly.

misconceptions.description: Mixes a loop with recursion and returns inside the loop, so only the first element is processed.
symptoms: return statement inside a for loop body in a recursive function
Result equals the value of the first element or first sublist only

misconceptions.description: Uses iteration where recursion is needed, handling a fixed nesting depth instead of arbitrary depth.
symptoms: Nested for loops with no recursive call
Passes flat and singly nested tests but fails deeper nesting
